1.title: Domain 1.0: General Security Concepts
1.summary: Covers foundational security controls, the CIA triad, authentication concepts, zero trust principles, physical safeguards, and core cryptographic standards tested on the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam.

objectives.title: Security Control Categories & Functional Types
objectives.overview: Security controls are safeguards deployed to avoid, detect, counteract, or minimize security risks to physical property, information systems, or organizational assets.

subtopics.title: 1. Implementation Categories (How Controls Are Implemented)
items: Technical (Logical) Controls: Hardware, software, or firmware mechanisms enforced by computer systems (e.g., firewall ACL rules, IDS/IPS signatures, endpoint anti-malware, database encryption, biometric readers, access control lists).

Managerial (Administrative) Controls: Strategic policies, compliance guidelines, administrative standards, and risk assessments established by executive leadership (e.g., Acceptable Use Policies, onboarding security checklists, periodic risk analysis, vendor governance).

Operational Controls: Everyday human-executed security practices and operational procedures (e.g., conducting backup restoration drills, routine log audits, security awareness training, visitor escort routines, physical guard patrols).

Physical Controls: Tangible barriers protecting facilities, perimeters, cabling, and computing hardware from physical intrusion or environmental disaster (e.g., perimeter fences, bollards, access control vestibules, security badges, CCTV cameras, server rack locks).

subtopics.title: 2. Functional Types (The Goal and Purpose of the Control)
items: Preventive Controls: Stop a security incident or unauthorized action before it can occur (e.g., IPS dropping malicious packets, firewalls blocking unauthorized ports, mantrap doors preventing tailgating, disabling USB ports).

Detective Controls: Identify, record, and alert on unauthorized activities during or immediately following an incident (e.g., IDS packet inspection, SIEM alert correlations, CCTV recordings, motion sensors, audit log reviews).

Corrective Controls: Remediate damage, eradicate threats, and restore systems to active operational baselines after a disruption (e.g., restoring files from clean immutable backups, quarantining infected endpoints, applying security patches).

Compensating Controls: Alternative or secondary safeguards deployed when primary controls are technically unfeasible or cost-prohibitive (e.g., isolating legacy SCADA equipment on an isolated VLAN with strict ACLs when it cannot support modern cipher suites).

Deterrent Controls: Discourage threat actors from attempting attacks by elevating perceived difficulty, visibility, or legal consequences (e.g., visible warning banners at logon, guard dogs, brightly lit perimeter fences, prominent surveillance signage).

Directive Controls: Mandate compliance with specific organizational rules, legal statutes, or operational standards (e.g., clean desk policies, regulatory compliance manuals, mandatory privacy training certifications).

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: CompTIA questions will ask you to classify a single mechanism under both Category and Function. For example: A biometric fingerprint door lock is Technical (Category) + Physical (Category) + Preventive (Function). A security policy is Managerial (Category) + Directive (Function).

objectives.title: Fundamental Security Concepts (CIA, Non-Repudiation, AAA)
objectives.overview: The core pillars governing information assurance, identity validation, and architectural posture across enterprise environments.

subtopics.title: 1. The CIA Triad
items: Confidentiality: Ensuring data is accessible solely by authorized personnel, processes, or devices. Enforced via AES-256 encryption at rest, TLS 1.3 in transit, role-based access control (RBAC), and strict data masking.

Integrity: Guaranteeing information has not been altered, deleted, or tampered with by unauthorized parties or system corruption. Enforced via cryptographic hash functions (SHA-256, SHA-3), digital signatures, and file integrity monitoring (FIM).

Availability: Ensuring systems, networks, and data remain reliably accessible to authorized users whenever needed. Enforced via redundant power supplies (UPS, generators), RAID disk arrays, load balancers, geographic failover clusters, and resilient backups.

subtopics.title: 2. Non-Repudiation & The AAA Framework
items: Non-Repudiation: The cryptographic proof that an entity performed a specific transaction or created a message, preventing them from denying authenticity. Achieved through asymmetric digital signatures combined with trusted PKI time-stamping.
Authentication (AuthN): Verifying the claimed identity of a user, service, or system through verified credentials (e.g., username/password, FIDO2 WebAuthn token, biometric scan).
Authorization (AuthZ): Determining the exact resources, permissions, and privileges granted to an authenticated identity (e.g., read, write, execute permissions via ACLs or ABAC).
Accounting (Auditing): Chronologically tracking, logging, and monitoring user activities, timestamps, resource consumption, and system events (e.g., SIEM logs, RADIUS accounting packets).

subtopics.title: 3. Security Posture Analysis
items: Gap Analysis: Formal evaluation comparing current security controls against an established industry benchmark (e.g., NIST CSF, ISO 27001) to identify defensive shortfalls.

Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA): Security philosophy eliminating implicit trust based on network location. Tenet: 'Never trust, always verify'. Requires explicit validation of every user, device, and payload.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: Hashing alone provides Integrity, but hashing does NOT provide Non-Repudiation unless combined with a private key (Digital Signature). Authentication happens BEFORE Authorization, and Accounting records what was done.

objectives.title: Zero Trust Architecture & Control Principles
objectives.overview: NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust defines an enterprise defense strategy that assumes breach, verifies every access request explicitly, and enforces least privilege dynamically.

subtopics.title: 1. Core Zero Trust Tenets
items: Assume Breach: Operate under the assumption that adversaries already have a foothold within the internal network perimeter.
Verify Explicitly: Authenticate and authorize based on all available data points (user identity, location, device health/compliance, service context, and anomalous behavior).
Least Privilege Access: Limit user and service access with Just-In-Time (JIT) and Just-Enough-Access (JEA) models, adaptive risk-based policies, and data protection.

subtopics.title: 2. Zero Trust Logical Architecture Components
items: Policy Decision Point (PDP): The central brain that evaluates access requests against security policies and threat intelligence. Consists of the Policy Engine and Policy Administrator.
Policy Enforcement Point (PEP): The gatekeeper (e.g., gateway, reverse proxy, host agent) that intercepts, enables, monitors, and terminates session connections based on PDP instructions.
Data Plane vs. Control Plane: Control Plane coordinates policy and routing instructions; Data Plane handles the actual transport and inspection of application payloads.
Microsegmentation: Dividing network workloads and application tiers into isolated security zones protected by individual PEPs to prevent lateral attacker movement.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: In CompTIA questions, legacy perimeter security (firewalls guarding the castle while inside is trusted) is always contrasted with Zero Trust. Zero Trust requires microsegmentation and continuous verification via PDP and PEP.

objectives.title: Physical & Environmental Security Controls
objectives.overview: Defending physical facilities, server rooms, cabling conduits, and endpoints against unauthorized human access, natural disaster, and environmental failure.

subtopics.title: 1. Perimeter & Facility Outer Defenses
items: Bollards: Heavy concrete, steel, or hydraulic posts designed to prevent vehicle ram-raids into facility entrances.
Fences & Gates: Physical boundary barriers sized to deter casual trespassers (typically 8 feet / 2.4 meters with barbed wire for high security).
Security Guards & Roving Patrols: Human presence capable of adaptive decision-making, physical intervention, and credential inspection.
Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV): Cameras positioned at entrances, perimeters, and server rooms for real-time monitoring and forensic review.

subtopics.title: 2. Building & Server Room Interior Controls
items: Access Control Vestibules (Mantraps): Two-door interlocking entry systems where Door B cannot open until Door A closes and authenticates, defeating tailgating and piggybacking.
Biometric Scanners: Fingerprint, iris, retina, or facial recognition devices authenticating physiological attributes at high-security server rooms.
Faraday Cages & Shielded Conduits: Metallic enclosures or cabling sheaths that block electromagnetic emissions and eavesdropping (TEMPEST standard).

Airflow Management & Fire Suppression: Hot-aisle/cold-aisle server rack alignment for thermal efficiency; clean-agent gas suppression (FM-200, Novec 1230) replacing water sprinklers to protect running electronics.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: Differentiate Tailgating vs Piggybacking. Tailgating is an unauthorized person slipping through a door behind an authorized user WITHOUT their knowledge. Piggybacking is when the authorized user willingly holds the door for the unauthorized person.

objectives.title: Cryptographic Concepts, Algorithms & PKI
objectives.overview: Mathematical algorithms and public key infrastructure protecting confidentiality, ensuring integrity, and verifying non-repudiation across digital communications.

subtopics.title: 1. Symmetric Encryption Algorithms (Single Shared Secret Key)
items: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard): NIST standard symmetric block cipher (128, 192, 256-bit keys). Extremely fast, hardware-accelerated. Standard for data at rest and TLS payloads.
ChaCha20: High-speed 256-bit stream cipher optimized for software implementations lacking dedicated AES CPU acceleration (commonly paired with Poly1305 in mobile TLS).
3DES / DES: Legacy block ciphers using 64-bit blocks. Deprecated due to short key lengths and Sweet32 vulnerability.

Symmetric Modes of Operation: GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) provides authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD); CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) requires initialization vectors (IV) but is vulnerable to padding oracle attacks.

subtopics.title: 2. Asymmetric Cryptography (Public / Private Key Pairs)
items: RSA: Factoring large prime numbers (2048, 4096-bit keys). Used for digital signatures, identity verification, and legacy key transport.

ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography): Uses algebraic curves to provide equivalent security to RSA with significantly smaller key sizes (e.g., 256-bit ECC ≈ 3072-bit RSA), making it ideal for mobile and IoT devices.

Diffie-Hellman (DH / ECDHE): Asymmetric key exchange protocol enabling two parties to establish a shared symmetric secret over an untrusted channel. Ephemeral DH (DHE/ECDHE) ensures Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS).

subtopics.title: 3. Cryptographic Hashing & Key Stretching
items: SHA-2 & SHA-3: Secure Hash Algorithms (SHA-256, SHA-512) generating one-way fixed-length digests for file integrity and digital signatures.
MD5 & SHA-1: Cryptographically broken hash functions vulnerable to collision attacks (two distinct inputs producing the identical hash digest). Deprecated.
Key Stretching: Slowing down password hashing to defeat brute-force and rainbow table attacks. Examples: PBKDF2, bcrypt, and Argon2.

subtopics.title: 4. Public Key Infrastructure (PKI)
items: Certificate Authority (CA): Trusted entity that issues, signs, and revokes digital certificates binding public keys to identities.

CRL vs. OCSP: CRL (Certificate Revocation List) is a published list of revoked serial numbers (can be large and outdated); OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) checks revocation status in real-time. OCSP Stapling allows the web server to query the CA and attach the signed status directly to the TLS handshake, reducing latency.
Certificate Formats: .pem (Base64 ASCII), .der (binary format), .pfx / .p12 (PKCS#12 holding public certificate and private key with password protection), .cer / .crt (public certificate only).

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: Digital Signatures use the SENDER'S PRIVATE KEY to encrypt the hash. Anyone with the sender's public key can verify integrity and authenticity. Asymmetric encryption for confidentiality uses the RECIPIENT'S PUBLIC KEY so only the recipient can decrypt with their private key.

2.title: Domain 2.0: Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations
2.summary: Covers threat actor profiles, attack vectors, social engineering, vulnerability analysis, malware strains, indicators of compromise (IoCs), and defensive mitigation strategies.

objectives.title: Threat Actor Profiles, Attributes & Motivations
objectives.overview: Understanding adversary origins, capabilities, resources, and intents is crucial for accurate threat modeling and proactive defensive posture.

subtopics.title: 1. Threat Actor Classifications
items: Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) / Nation-State: Government-backed actors possessing virtually unlimited funding, elite technical sophistication, and extreme patience. Motivated by geopolitical espionage, intellectual property theft, and infrastructure disruption.
Organized Crime / Cybercriminals: Highly structured illicit enterprises motivated primarily by immediate financial gain (e.g., Ransomware-as-a-Service [RaaS], BEC wire fraud, carding).
Insider Threats: Current or former employees, contractors, or business partners with authorized access who abuse privileges maliciously or cause breaches inadvertently due to negligence.
Hacktivists: Individuals or loosely organized groups launching cyber attacks to promote ideological, environmental, political, or social causes (e.g., defacement, DDoS).
Script Kiddies: Inexperienced threat actors utilizing publicly available exploit scripts, pre-built attack frameworks, and automated tools without understanding underlying mechanics.
Shadow IT: Employees deploying unauthorized software, cloud services, or hardware to circumvent IT friction, inadvertently creating unmonitored attack vectors.

subtopics.title: 2. Threat Actor Attributes & Vectors
items: Internal vs. External: Internal actors already reside inside the trust perimeter with valid credentials; external actors must breach perimeter boundaries.
Resource & Sophistication Level: Ranging from low (script kiddies) to nation-state level (custom zero-day exploits, hardware supply chain interdiction).
Intent & Motivation: Financial, political, personal grievance, competitive advantage, sabotage, or philosophical alignment.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: CompTIA loves testing Insider Threats. An insider does NOT need to be malicious; an employee who misconfigures an S3 cloud storage bucket or clicks a phishing link is also categorized under insider threat vulnerability.

objectives.title: Attack Vectors & Enterprise Attack Surfaces
objectives.overview: An attack vector is the specific path or pipeline through which a threat actor gains unauthorized access; the attack surface is the total sum of all vulnerable entry points.

subtopics.title: 1. Common Attack Vectors
items: Email & Messaging: The primary vector for initial access via malicious attachments (macros, HTML smuggling), weaponized URLs, and business email compromise (BEC).
Supply Chain: Compromising trusted third-party software updates, hardware vendors, or managed service providers (MSPs) to infiltrate downstream customer networks (e.g., SolarWinds breach).
Removable Media: Physical USB flash drive drops, autorun exploits, or malicious charging cables (e.g., O.MG cable) circumventing air gaps.
Cloud Infrastructure: Publicly exposed object storage buckets (AWS S3), overly permissive IAM service roles, unauthenticated APIs, and unpatched container images.
Wireless Networks: Rogue Access Points, Evil Twin Wi-Fi clones mimicking corporate SSIDs, captive portal credential harvesters, and outdated WPA2 implementations.

subtopics.title: 2. Attack Surface Reduction Strategies
items: Disabling Unused Ports & Protocols: Closing non-essential services (Telnet 23, FTP 21, SMB 445 on internet boundaries).
Principle of Least Functionality: Configuring operating systems and server baselines to execute only applications strictly necessary for business roles.
Asset Management & Shadow IT Discovery: Continuous automated scanning to identify rogue servers, orphan cloud workloads, and unmanaged devices.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: If an exam scenario describes an attacker targeting a heating/cooling vendor or software library to breach a major retailer, the correct answer is Supply Chain Attack.

objectives.title: Social Engineering Techniques & Psychological Triggers
objectives.overview: Social engineering exploits human psychology rather than software vulnerabilities to manipulate individuals into disclosing credentials or executing unauthorized actions.

subtopics.title: 1. Targeted Social Engineering Types
items: Phishing: Broad, untargeted mass emails masquerading as reputable brands to harvest login credentials or distribute malware.
Spear Phishing: Customized, researched email attacks targeting specific individuals or organizations utilizing personal details.
Whaling: High-level spear phishing targeting C-suite executives, board members, or financial controllers to execute high-value wire transfers.
Vishing & Smishing: Voice phishing conducted over phone systems (often spoofing caller ID); Smishing conducted via SMS text messages.
Pretexting: Constructing an elaborate fabricated scenario (e.g., pretending to be an external auditor or HR specialist) to coax sensitive information from an employee.
Watering Hole Attack: Compromising a legitimate website known to be frequented by a specific target group, poisoning it with drive-by malware.

Physical Social Engineering: Shoulder surfing (looking over screens), Dumpster diving (retrieving discarded paper notes), Tailgating (unauthorized trailing), and Baiting (leaving infected USB drives in parking lots).

subtopics.title: 2. Psychological Principles Exploited
items: Urgency: Manufacturing a false deadline ('Account suspended in 15 minutes!') to bypass rational caution.
Authority: Impersonating executives, legal counsel, or police officers to compel compliance.
Fear & Intimidation: Threatening disciplinary action, legal prosecution, or job loss.
Social Proof / Consensus: Convincing the victim that colleagues have already complied with the request.
Familiarity / Liking: Establishing rapport and mutual interests before making an illicit request.
Scarcity & Greed: Promising exclusive financial windfalls or gift cards.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: If an attacker gathers public intelligence about an executive's travel schedule from LinkedIn and targets the corporate treasurer with an urgent invoice payment, that is Whaling + Spear Phishing exploiting Urgency and Authority.

objectives.title: Software Vulnerabilities, Application Flaws & Memory Exploits
objectives.overview: Flaws in software design, implementation, configuration, or memory management that allow attackers to bypass security boundaries or execute arbitrary code.

subtopics.title: 1. Web Application Vulnerabilities
items: SQL Injection (SQLi): Malicious SQL statements injected into input fields to query, alter, or dump backend database tables. Mitigated by Parameterized Queries / Prepared Statements and input validation allowlists.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): Injecting client-side JavaScript executed within a victim's browser session. Types: Stored (in DB), Reflected (in URL parameters), DOM-based. Mitigated by context-aware output encoding and Content Security Policy (CSP).

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF): Coercing an authenticated victim browser into submitting unauthorized transactions to a trusted site. Mitigated by Anti-CSRF Synchronizer Tokens and SameSite=Strict cookies.

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF): Forcing a backend server to retrieve internal, unauthorized resources (such as AWS EC2 metadata at 169.254.169.254). Mitigated by strict URL allowlists and AWS IMDSv2 token enforcement.

subtopics.title: 2. Memory & System Software Exploits
items: Buffer Overflow: Writing data past allocated memory boundaries, overwriting adjacent memory and return pointers to hijack instruction execution. Mitigated by ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization), DEP / NX bit, and stack canaries.
Race Condition / TOCTOU: Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use flaw where state changes between permission verification and resource access, allowing unauthorized modification.
Memory Leaks: Failure to release allocated RAM, eventually exhausting system resources and causing denial-of-service crashes.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: The absolute #1 defense against SQL Injection is Parameterized Queries / Prepared Statements. The #1 defense against XSS is Context-Aware Output Encoding. The #1 defense against Buffer Overflows in legacy C applications is ASLR and DEP.

objectives.title: Malware Strains, Network Attacks & Indicators of Compromise (IoCs)
objectives.overview: Recognizing active malicious code types, network-level exploitation tactics, and technical indicators signifying ongoing system compromise.

subtopics.title: 1. Malware Strains & Taxonomy
items: Ransomware: Encrypts victim storage and databases, demanding cryptocurrency payment for decryption keys; modern strains employ double-extortion (exfiltrating data prior to encryption).
Trojans: Programs masquerading as benign utilities (e.g., game crack, PDF reader) that secretly execute unauthorized payloads.
Remote Access Trojans (RATs): Specialized trojans providing persistent interactive command-line, GUI, webcam, and microphone control to threat actors.
Worms: Self-replicating, self-propagating malware that travels across networks autonomously without user interaction by exploiting unpatched services.
Rootkits: Kernel-level or firmware-level stealth malware that replaces system binaries to hide its own presence, active processes, and open network sockets.
Living-off-the-Land (LotL) / Fileless Malware: Malicious scripts (PowerShell, WMI, bash) executed entirely in RAM without dropping standalone executable binaries onto disk.

subtopics.title: 2. Network Layer Attacks & Indicators
items: ARP Poisoning: Broadcasting forged ARP replies mapping an attacker MAC to the default gateway IP. Mitigated by Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on switches.
DNS Poisoning: Injecting fraudulent IP resolutions into recursive resolver caches. Mitigated by DNSSEC cryptographic signing.
On-Path (MITM) / Replay: Covert interception of network traffic between two parties. Mitigated by Mutual TLS (mTLS) and Perfect Forward Secrecy.
Beaconing: Regular, heartbeat-like HTTP/HTTPS outbound callbacks from compromised endpoints to Command & Control (C2) servers at fixed or jittered intervals.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: If malware hides by injecting code into Windows svchost.exe and executing via PowerShell in memory without files on disk, it is Fileless Malware (Living off the Land). If it modifies the OS kernel to hide running processes, it is a Rootkit.

objectives.title: Defensive Mitigation Techniques & Enterprise Hardening
objectives.overview: Tactical technical safeguards deployed across networks, operating systems, and applications to eliminate vulnerabilities and curtail attacker blast radius.

subtopics.title: 1. Infrastructure & Network Mitigations
items: Network Segmentation: Isolating network zones via VLANs, internal firewalls, and air gaps to restrict lateral movement.
Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) & DHCP Snooping: Switch security features preventing ARP poisoning and rogue DHCP servers by validating packet bindings.
DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions): Cryptographically signs DNS records with public key cryptography to guarantee authenticity and prevent cache poisoning.

subtopics.title: 2. Host & Endpoint Hardening
items: Patch Management: Systematic scanning, testing, and deployment of security updates (following a defined testing window before production push).
Endpoint Detection & Response (EDR / XDR): Behavioral analytics agents running on endpoints detecting anomalous process creation, memory injection, and LotL activity.
Application Allowlisting: Restricting systems to run only pre-approved, digitally signed executable binaries (e.g., AppLocker, Windows Defender Application Control).

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: Application Allowlisting (preventing unknown software from executing) is vastly superior to blocklisting (trying to keep up with millions of malware hashes). Allowlisting is the recommended mitigation against zero-day malware execution.

3.title: Domain 3.0: Security Architecture
3.summary: Covers cloud infrastructure models, boundary defense devices, data protection in all states, resilience, high availability, and modern identity/federation architecture.

objectives.title: Cloud Computing Models, SASE & Shared Responsibility
objectives.overview: Understanding how security accountability shifts between customers and cloud service providers across IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, and edge architectures.

subtopics.title: 1. Cloud Service Models (The Shared Responsibility Matrix)
items: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): CSP manages physical facilities, servers, and hypervisor. Customer is responsible for Guest OS, security patching, network configuration, applications, and data protection (e.g., AWS EC2, Azure VMs).
Platform as a Service (PaaS): CSP manages physical infrastructure, hypervisor, OS, and runtime environment. Customer manages application source code and data (e.g., AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Heroku).

Software as a Service (SaaS): CSP manages the entire technology stack. Customer is responsible solely for data access permissions, user identity, and security configuration settings (e.g., Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Salesforce).

subtopics.title: 2. SASE & Cloud Security Solutions
items: SASE (Secure Access Service Edge): Architectural framework combining software-defined networking (SD-WAN) with cloud-delivered security services at distributed edge points of presence (PoPs).

CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker): Policy enforcement point between enterprise users and cloud services. Deployed in API Mode (out-of-band audit, configuration compliance) or Inline Proxy Mode (forward/reverse proxy for real-time DLP and threat prevention).
FWaaS & SWG: Cloud-hosted Next-Gen Firewalls and Secure Web Gateways filtering traffic for remote branch offices without backhauling traffic over MPLS.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: Under the Shared Responsibility Model, DATA is ALWAYS the customer's responsibility across IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. Physical datacenter security is ALWAYS the cloud provider's responsibility.

objectives.title: Enterprise Network Infrastructure & Boundary Security
objectives.overview: Designing defense-in-depth perimeter architectures using modern firewalls, intrusion inspection engines, proxies, and segmented zones.

subtopics.title: 1. Firewalls & Traffic Inspection
items: Packet-Filtering Firewalls: Layer 3/4 stateless filters evaluating individual packets against IP and port ACL rules independently.
Stateful Firewalls: Tracks active connection states in a state table, automatically permitting established return traffic without explicit inbound rules.
Next-Generation Firewalls (NGFW): Layer 7 deep packet inspection (DPI) engines capable of identifying specific applications, decrypting TLS traffic, and enforcing IPS rules regardless of port used.
Web Application Firewalls (WAF): Layer 7 proxy specifically inspecting HTTP/HTTPS traffic for web exploits (SQLi, XSS, CSRF, directory traversal).

subtopics.title: 2. Network Zones & Proxies
items: Demilitarized Zone (DMZ): An isolated perimeter network housing public-facing servers (web, mail, reverse proxy) buffered between external internet and internal LAN.

Forward Proxy vs. Reverse Proxy: Forward Proxy sits in front of internal clients to inspect and filter outbound web traffic; Reverse Proxy sits in front of internal web servers to provide load balancing, SSL termination, and caching.
Jump Box (Bastion Host): A hardened, isolated server used by administrators to securely manage internal systems inside sensitive network zones via SSH or RDP with mandatory MFA.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: A standard network firewall cannot inspect encrypted HTTPS traffic or detect SQL injection payloads hidden inside port 443 web requests. A Web Application Firewall (WAF) or NGFW with SSL/TLS decryption is required.

objectives.title: Data Protection States, Cryptographic Lifecycle & Resilience
objectives.overview: Safeguarding corporate data throughout its operational lifecycle and building resilient architectures to ensure high availability and disaster recovery.

subtopics.title: 1. The Three States of Data
items: Data at Rest: Inactive data stored in databases, hard drives, SANs, or backup tapes. Protected by Full Disk Encryption (FDE / BitLocker), self-encrypting drives (SED), and AES-256 database encryption.
Data in Transit (Motion): Data traversing internal or external networks. Protected by TLS 1.3, IPsec VPN tunnels, and HTTPS.
Data in Use: Active data residing in volatile memory (RAM, CPU cache, registers). Protected by confidential computing (hardware enclaves / SGX) and secure memory segmentation.

subtopics.title: 2. Data Loss Prevention (DLP) & Obfuscation
items: DLP (Data Loss Prevention): Systems scanning email, USB transfers, and cloud uploads for sensitive patterns (SSNs, credit card numbers, confidential tags) to block unauthorized exfiltration.
Tokenization: Replacing sensitive data (e.g., credit card numbers) with a randomly generated, non-sensitive token value mapped in a secure token vault.
Data Masking: Obfuscating sensitive fields in non-production environments (e.g., replacing credit card digits with XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-1234).

subtopics.title: 3. Storage Resilience & High Availability
items: RAID 0 (Striping): High performance, 0 fault tolerance. If 1 disk fails, all data is lost.
RAID 1 (Mirroring): Complete duplicate copy across 2 disks. Survives 1 disk failure (50% usable capacity).
RAID 5 (Striping + Distributed Parity): Minimum 3 disks. Survives 1 disk failure. Usable capacity is N - 1 disks.
RAID 6 (Dual Distributed Parity): Minimum 4 disks. Survives up to 2 simultaneous disk failures. Usable capacity is N - 2 disks.
RAID 10 (1+0 Striped Mirrors): Minimum 4 disks. Combines high performance of striping with fault tolerance of mirroring. Survives 1 disk failure per mirror pair.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: Tokenization replaces data with a non-mathematical placeholder and cannot be reversed without the token database. Encryption uses a mathematical algorithm with a cryptographic key and can be reversed by anyone possessing the key.

objectives.title: Identity, Access Management & Federation Architecture
objectives.overview: Architecting secure identification, multifactor authentication, directory federation, and access control models across enterprise ecosystems.

subtopics.title: 1. Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) Factors
items: Something You Know: Passwords, passphrases, PINs (least secure, vulnerable to phishing and brute-force).
Something You Have: Hardware security tokens (YubiKey), smartphone authenticator apps (TOTP), smart cards.
Something You Are: Biometric attributes (fingerprint, facial geometry, retina, iris).
Somewhere You Are: Geolocation, IP address range, GPS coordinates.
Something You Do: Keystroke dynamics, signature cadence, gait analysis.

subtopics.title: 2. Federation & Single Sign-On (SSO) Protocols
items: SAML 2.0: XML-based framework exchanging authentication and authorization assertions between an Identity Provider (IdP) and Service Provider (SP). Dominant for enterprise SaaS web SSO.
OAuth 2.0: JSON/REST authorization framework enabling third-party applications to access resources on behalf of a user using scoped Access Tokens and Refresh Tokens (delegation, not authN).
OpenID Connect (OIDC): Identity authentication layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 issuing signed JSON Web Tokens (JWT ID tokens) to authenticate users.
SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management): Standardized JSON/REST protocol automating user account provisioning, role updates, and de-provisioning between IdPs and cloud applications.

subtopics.title: 3. Access Control Models
items: DAC (Discretionary Access Control): Resource owner determines permissions (e.g., standard NTFS or Linux permissions). Flexible but high administrative overhead.
MAC (Mandatory Access Control): Access enforced by the OS based on security classification labels (Top Secret, Secret) and user clearances. Non-discretionary (military, SELinux).
RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): Access assigned based on organizational job roles and functions. Follows Principle of Least Privilege.

ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): Dynamic policies evaluated based on Subject, Resource, Action, and Environmental context (device health, IP risk, time of day). The access foundation of Zero Trust.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: Two passwords or a password + PIN is NOT MFA; that is Single-Factor Authentication (two of 'Something You Know'). MFA requires at least TWO DIFFERENT CATEGORIES (e.g., password [know] + smartphone push notification [have]).

4.title: Domain 4.0: Security Operations
4.summary: The largest domain on the exam (28%). Covers security baselines, monitoring tools (SIEM/SOAR), vulnerability assessments, pen testing, incident response playbooks, and digital forensics.

objectives.title: Security Baselines, Instrumentation & Monitoring Tools
objectives.overview: Implementing visibility and telemetry across networks, endpoints, and applications to detect anomalies and orchestrate rapid response.

subtopics.title: 1. Centralized Telemetry & Analysis Platforms
items: SIEM (Security Information & Event Management): Aggregates, normalizes, and correlates log data across thousands of systems to detect anomalous security events in real-time.

SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response): Ingests alerts from SIEMs and automates incident remediation tasks through automated Playbooks and Runbooks (e.g., automatically isolating an infected host or disabling compromised user credentials).
EDR / XDR: Endpoint Detection and Response tools monitoring endpoint behavioral telemetry; XDR extends detection across network, cloud, email, and identity data streams.
User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA): Machine learning baselines tracking normal user activity to detect insider anomalies (e.g., downloading gigabytes of data at 3 AM from an unusual IP).

subtopics.title: 2. Network Protocol Analyzers & Scanners
items: Packet Analyzers (Wireshark, tcpdump): Captures and inspects raw packet payloads at the byte level for diagnostic protocol inspection.
NetFlow / IPFIX: Collects flow metadata (source/destination IP, ports, protocol, bytes transferred) without storing full packet payloads, enabling scalable bandwidth and anomaly analysis.
Network Scanners (Nmap): Network discovery tool identifying live hosts, open TCP/UDP ports, operating system fingerprints, and running service versions.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: SIEM alerts human analysts to an incident; SOAR executes automated scripts (Playbooks) to remediate the incident automatically without human intervention.

objectives.title: Vulnerability Management, Scanning & Penetration Testing
objectives.overview: Proactively identifying system flaws, prioritizing remediation through standard vulnerability scoring, and validating defensive depth through simulated attacks.

subtopics.title: 1. Vulnerability Assessment & Scanning
items: Credentialed vs. Non-Credentialed Scans: Credentialed scans log into the host with valid credentials to inspect installed software, patch revisions, and configuration files (low false positives); Non-credentialed scans simulate external attackers probing open network ports from outside (higher false positives).

CVE & CVSS: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) provides standard flaw identifiers; Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) scores severity from 0.0 to 10.0 based on exploitability, attack vector, and impact.

False Positives vs. False Negatives: False Positive is a scanner alerting on a vulnerability that does NOT actually exist; False Negative is a scanner failing to detect a critical vulnerability that DOES exist (far more dangerous).

subtopics.title: 2. Penetration Testing Methodologies
items: Penetration Testing Phases: Scoping & Rules of Engagement $\to$ Passive/Active Reconnaissance $\to$ Vulnerability Analysis $\to$ Exploitation $\to$ Lateral Movement / Privilege Escalation $\to$ Reporting.

Target Knowledge Levels: Black Box (zero prior internal knowledge, blind external view), White Box (full architectural diagrams, source code, credentials provided), Gray Box (partial knowledge provided).
Security Exercises: Red Team (offensive attack simulation), Blue Team (defensive detection and response), Purple Team (collaborative debriefing and joint defensive hardening).

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: A Vulnerability Scan is passive and automated—it identifies and reports potential flaws without exploiting them. A Penetration Test actively attempts to exploit vulnerabilities to verify real-world compromise.

objectives.title: Identity & Access Management Operations & Account Auditing
objectives.overview: Managing the full identity lifecycle, enforcing least privilege, conducting access reviews, and configuring robust password and authentication policies.

subtopics.title: 1. Identity Lifecycle Management
items: Account Provisioning: Automating user onboarding and privilege assignments according to job department via HR connectors (SCIM).
Privilege Creep & Access Reviews: Periodic auditing of employee privileges to revoke access rights accumulated as roles change over time.
Offboarding & Account Deprovisioning: Immediately disabling account credentials, terminating active sessions, and revoking PKI certificates upon employee departure.

subtopics.title: 2. Administrative Account Protections
items: Privileged Access Management (PAM): Vaulting domain administrative credentials with check-in/check-out access, session recording, and automated password rotation.

Service Accounts & gMSA: Non-human accounts running background daemons; Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) automatically manage complex 128-character Kerberos passwords in Active Directory, preventing Kerberoasting.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: When an employee leaves the company, NEVER delete the account immediately; DISABLE the account first to preserve file ownership and audit logs while immediately blocking authentication.

objectives.title: Incident Response Lifecycle (PICERL) & Digital Forensics
objectives.overview: Executing structured incident triage protocols to contain threats and gathering admissible legal evidence according to established digital forensics standards.

subtopics.title: 1. NIST / CompTIA Incident Response Lifecycle (PICERL)
items: 1. Preparation: Developing playbooks, assembling IR jump kits, establishing communication channels, and conducting tabletop simulation exercises.
2. Identification: Detecting security events, triaging alerts, and determining the scope and severity of compromise.
3. Containment: Isolating compromised hosts (network quarantine) or segmenting subnets to stop adversary spread while preserving volatile memory.
4. Eradication: Removing malware, terminating illicit user accounts, closing exploited vulnerabilities, and wiping affected systems.
5. Recovery: Restoring systems from verified clean backups, validating operational stability, and reconnecting systems to production with enhanced monitoring.
6. Lessons Learned: Conducting post-incident debriefings within two weeks to update policies, improve response times, and prevent recurrence.

subtopics.title: 2. RFC 3227 Order of Volatility (Capture Sequence)
items: 1. CPU Registers and CPU Cache (lost in nanoseconds upon power disruption).
2. Routing Table, ARP Cache, Process Table, Kernel Statistics, RAM (lost in microseconds to minutes).
3. Temporary File Systems, Swap Space, Paging Files (lost upon reboot).
4. Disk Storage / Non-Volatile Media (persistent hard drives, SSDs, USB drives).
5. Remote Logging and SIEM Data (stored on dedicated off-target log servers).
6. Physical Network Configuration and Cabling Topology.
7. Archival Media (backup tapes, optical media, cold storage).

subtopics.title: 3. Digital Forensics Integrity Standards
items: Chain of Custody: Meticulous chronological documentation recording who collected, handled, transferred, analyzed, and secured digital evidence to ensure court admissibility.
Legal Hold: Formal directive ordering suspension of routine data destruction and automated document purging when litigation is anticipated.
Hardware Write Blockers: Physical bridge devices preventing any write modifications to evidence storage media during bit-stream image acquisition.
Cryptographic Hash Verification: Calculating SHA-256 hashes immediately before and after imaging; matching hashes prove bit-for-bit evidence integrity.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: If an investigator arrives at an infected, running computer, NEVER power it off or reboot it! Powering off destroys live RAM, active network sockets, decrypted encryption keys, and process tables. Capture RAM FIRST!

5.title: Domain 5.0: Security Program Management and Oversight
5.summary: Covers enterprise risk management, quantitative risk formulas (ALE/SLE), privacy regulations (GDPR/HIPAA), security frameworks (NIST/ISO/SOC 2), and third-party vendor oversight.

objectives.title: Governance, Enterprise Risk Management & Quantitative Formulas
objectives.overview: Quantifying organizational threats, balancing risk tolerance, calculating financial exposure, and executing strategic business continuity planning.

subtopics.title: 1. Quantitative Risk Management Formulas
items: SLE (Single Loss Expectancy): Financial loss occurring from a single security incident. Formula: SLE = Asset Value (AV) × Exposure Factor (EF).
ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence): The estimated frequency or number of times an incident is anticipated to occur within a single year.
ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy): Expected monetary loss incurred per year. Formula: ALE = SLE × ARO.
Cost-Benefit Analysis: The annual cost of a security safeguard must NOT exceed the reduction in ALE: Cost of Safeguard < (ALE_before - ALE_after).

subtopics.title: 2. Risk Handling Strategies
items: Risk Mitigation: Implementing security controls to reduce likelihood or impact (e.g., installing a firewall, deploying EDR).
Risk Transference: Offloading financial impact to a third party (e.g., purchasing cyber insurance, outsourcing datacenter hosting to a cloud provider).
Risk Acceptance: Acknowledging risk and operating without additional controls because the cost of mitigation exceeds potential loss.
Risk Avoidance: Completely eliminating the risk by terminating the activity or shutting down the vulnerable system.

subtopics.title: 3. Business Impact Analysis (BIA) Metrics
items: RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Maximum acceptable duration a system or service can remain offline before catastrophic business impact occurs.
RPO (Recovery Point Objective): Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time (e.g., an RPO of 2 hours requires database backups every 2 hours).
MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures): Expected operational lifespan of a repairable component between failure events.
MTTR (Mean Time to Repair): Average time required to diagnose, repair, and restore a failed system to full production.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: If Asset Value = $100,000, Exposure Factor = 25%, and incident occurs once every 2 years (ARO = 0.5): SLE = $100,000 × 0.25 = $25,000. ALE = $25,000 × 0.5 = $12,500. A safeguard costing $15,000/year should NOT be purchased!

objectives.title: Privacy Regulations, Legal Compliance & Data Protection Roles
objectives.overview: Navigating statutory privacy mandates, breach notification rules, and organizational data handling responsibilities.

subtopics.title: 1. Major Regulatory Mandates
items: GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation): European Union regulation protecting personal data. Mandates 72-hour breach notification to supervisory authorities, Right to Erasure ('Right to be Forgotten'), Data Protection Officer (DPO) requirement, and fines up to 4% global turnover.

HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act): US law protecting Protected Health Information (PHI). Mandates Security Rule (Administrative, Physical, Technical safeguards) and Business Associate Agreements (BAAs).

PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard): Technical standard protecting cardholder data (CHD). Requires PAN encryption, network segmentation, and quarterly scans by Approved Scanning Vendors (ASV).
SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley Act): US statute protecting investors against corporate accounting fraud by mandating strict internal IT controls over financial data systems.

subtopics.title: 2. Data Privacy Roles & Responsibilities
items: Data Owner: Senior executive accountable for classifying data, defining access rules, and overall compliance.
Data Controller: Organization determining the purpose and means of processing personal data under GDPR.
Data Processor: Third-party service processing personal data on behalf of the controller (e.g., cloud payroll provider).
Data Custodian (Steward): Technical staff implementing backups, encryption, and access controls as directed by the Data Owner.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: Know the difference between Data Owner (accountable for data classification and policies) vs Data Custodian (responsible for technical implementation, storage, and daily backups).

objectives.title: Security Frameworks, Industry Benchmarks & Operational Policies
objectives.overview: Adopting recognized defensive frameworks to structure enterprise security programs and establishing enforceable organizational policies.

subtopics.title: 1. Cybersecurity Frameworks
items: NIST CSF 2.0 (Cybersecurity Framework): Six foundational functions: Govern (GV), Identify (ID), Protect (PR), Detect (DE), Respond (RS), and Recover (RC).
ISO/IEC 27001 & 27002: International standard for establishing an Information Security Management System (ISMS); 27002 provides the practical code of practice for controls.

SOC 2 (Service Organization Control): AICPA audit evaluating 5 Trust Services Criteria (Security, Availability, Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy). Type I evaluates design at a point in time; Type II evaluates operational effectiveness over 6+ months.
CIS Critical Security Controls (v8): Prioritized list of 18 prescriptive, technical defensive safeguards focusing on high-impact cyber hygiene.

subtopics.title: 2. Essential Organizational Policies
items: Acceptable Use Policy (AUP): Defines permitted and prohibited activities when using corporate hardware, networks, and internet access.
Change Management Policy: Mandatory review, risk analysis, CAB approval, and rollback testing prior to implementing IT system modifications.
Clean Desk & Clear Screen Policy: Mandates locking screens and storing sensitive documents in locked drawers when unattended to defeat shoulder surfing.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: SOC 2 Type I is a snapshot report verifying that controls are designed properly today. SOC 2 Type II is a rigorous historical audit proving controls operated effectively across at least six months.

objectives.title: Third-Party & Supply Chain Risk Management
objectives.overview: Evaluating external vendors, securing hardware and software supply chains, and establishing enforceable legal service agreements.

subtopics.title: 1. Vendor Due Diligence & Assessment
items: Security Questionnaires: Assessing vendor security posture prior to contract signing (evaluating data handling, encryption, and employee vetting).
Right-to-Audit Clauses: Contractual provisions permitting customer security teams or independent auditors to inspect vendor facilities and systems.
Software Bill of Materials (SBOM): Comprehensive inventory of open-source and proprietary software components, libraries, and dependencies embedded in an application.

subtopics.title: 2. Inter-Organizational Legal Agreements
items: SLA (Service Level Agreement): Contractually binding document defining minimum performance metrics, service uptime guarantees (e.g., 99.99%), and financial penalties for outages.
MOU / MOA (Memorandum of Understanding / Agreement): Preliminary non-binding document establishing mutual intent and responsibilities between organizations.
ISA (Interconnection Security Agreement): Technical document detailing technical security requirements when connecting two distinct organizational networks.
BAA (Business Associate Agreement): Legally required HIPAA contract ensuring third-party vendors safeguard shared healthcare PHI.

objectives.exam_takeaway: Exam Watch: When two companies connect their internal networks via dedicated VPN or MPLS link, the technical requirements, encryption standards, and port allowances MUST be documented in an ISA (Interconnection Security Agreement).
